title: Pre-fill the action in a motive frame
statement: In a why-question's answer frame, print the character's action already, leaving only the reason to write, so the answer cannot just restate the action.
example: One lesson prints the procedure's three-part sentence with its first two parts filled, leaving only the conclusion to the child.
detail: Lesson research on motive questions for a grade 4 reading lesson describes a child who, asked why a character tied his men up, answers that he tied them up, staying at the word and phrase level that a literature review on inference finds in poorer comprehenders. Its design consequence is an answer slot that makes restating impossible: a sentence frame whose first half is already the action, so the only place left to write is the reason. The lesson plan adopts this at its guided step, printing the procedure's three-part sentence with the first two parts filled, which it says is what stops the child restating the action instead of inferring from it.
against: The research note calls the diagnosis its own: "The review does not name this failure directly, so treat the diagnosis as my own; what it does support is the cause and the fix." (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l3-circe-and-the-lotus-eaters.md`, lines 286-288). It was "Written before the lesson is authored." (line 9), and nothing records learners using the frame.

evidence.quote: A child who answers "because he tied them up" to "why did he tie them up" has stayed at that level. The design consequence is that the answer slot must make restating impossible: a sentence frame whose first half is already the action, so that the only place the child can write is the reason.
It is also the only shape that can print the procedure's own three-part sentence with the first two parts filled, which is what stops the child restating the action instead of inferring from it.
